---
title: "Make, Buy, or Reprice"
---


::: {.learning-objectives}
## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

After completing this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Classify a plant's conversion costs from the ledger and the production records into costs that vary with output, committed capacity costs, and the cost of capacity left unused, and test each classification against the data.
2. Compute standard, actual absorption, and time-driven costs for product families, and explain why the three disagree and which question each answers.
3. Evaluate a supplier's quote on relevant costs, separating the costs that stop from those that stay, and value the capacity that buying would free.
4. Analyze a price increase with contribution margins and the volume it can afford to lose, and judge the evidence on how customers respond to price.
5. Propose standard costs on a stated level of capacity, measure their effect on inventory and on statements already issued, and recommend how to report it.
6. Choose SQL, Excel, or Power BI for each step of an integrated analysis, and write a recommendation, family by family, that two decision makers who disagree can act on.
:::


::: {.chapter-slides data-chapter="chapter-18"}
:::

## Opening Scenario {.unnumbered}

It is August 2027. Reviewing the fiscal 2026 results, the CFO found one comparison that would not go away. Once the manufacturing variance is charged, the furniture Charles River makes earns about ten points less than its standard margin, while the furniture it buys earns about what its standards say. The CFO's reading is blunt. The plant applies overhead at little more than a third of what it costs, and neither list prices nor standard costs have changed in three years, so the standards understate what every manufactured product costs. Is Charles River selling below cost, and should it be making these products at all?

The production manager disagrees. The plant has room to spare, and idle capacity, in the production manager's words, is not the products' fault. To test the CFO's question, the purchasing manager asked a contract manufacturer to quote six of the families the plant makes, and the quote has arrived. It expires on 15 September, because the supplier needs the autumn to tool up for January deliveries, and the 2028 price list must go to customers on 1 October. The CFO and the production manager meet on 31 August to decide.

The controller asks you, the staff accountant, for the analysis and a decision memo. This chapter is a case, and it has no tutorials. Each requirement states what the decision needs and names the chapters it draws on, and you decide how to produce it. Where a tool is the clear choice, the requirement says why; elsewhere, choose and explain your choice in your documentation.


## The Situation

The CFO asks three questions:

- what each family costs to make, and which of those costs would stop if Charles River stopped making it;
- where the contract manufacturer is cheaper, whether Charles River should buy;
- where Charles River keeps making, what prices the 2028 list needs.

The production manager adds two:

- what happens to the plant's hours, its crew, and the costs that stay;
- whether the standards should change, and to what.

The controller sets five conditions. First, everyone works from the same assumptions, which she lists in @tbl-18-02. Second, every figure reconciles to the ledger: the manufacturing variance in account 5080 and the costs that flow into account 1090 Manufacturing Cost Clearing, which are the payroll, the Factory Overhead entries, and the depreciation charged to it, not the debits that favorable closes post back to it. Third, fiscal 2026 is the base year, because the records end there. Fourth, the decision is made family by family; the products Charles River buys in the same families are different products, not substitutes for the ones it makes. Fifth, decisions about positions belong to the production manager, so the memo states what a change in the crew would save and what it would cost, and leaves the decision there.

The quote is in @tbl-18-01. Its prices are averages per unit at the 2026 mix of items in each family. They are the case's assumption, set to resemble what Charles River pays for the products it already buys in those families, and they are not part of the dataset.

| Family | Quoted annual volume (units) | Average price per unit | One-time tooling and qualification | Lead time |
|-------------------|------------|------------|-------------|------------|
| FUR-BNH Benches | 1,450 | \$325 | \$18,000 | 8 weeks |
| FUR-NGT Nightstands | 3,200 | \$270 | \$22,000 | 8 weeks |
| FUR-SDB Sideboards | 3,800 | \$325 | \$25,000 | 8 weeks |
| FUR-TBL Dining tables | 5,000 | \$315 | \$30,000 | 8 weeks |
| LGT-SCN Wall sconces | 4,600 | \$180 | \$15,000 | 6 weeks |
| TXT-PIL Pillow covers | 700 | \$220 | \$8,000 | 6 weeks |

: The contract manufacturer's quote (a hypothetical exhibit) {#tbl-18-01}

The terms come with the prices. Prices are fixed for 2028 and 2029, and Charles River commits to buy at least 80% of the quoted volume of each family it chooses each year. The goods are sold at the supplier's plant, so Charles River pays inbound freight, which the purchasing manager estimates at 3% of price. The supplier builds to Charles River's designs and bills of material and credits defects above 1.5% of units, Charles River's quality assurance inspects samples on arrival, and payment is due in 45 days.

| Assumption | Value |
|-------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Base year | Fiscal 2026 |
| Practical capacity | 80% of the available hours in WorkCenterCalendar |
| Straight-time labor rate and burden | 26.62 an hour; burden 14.14% of pay |
| Hours per standard hour at plan | 1.18, of which 0.18 indirect |
| Plan volume, the normal capacity | 68,912.79 standard hours a year |
| Salaried production staff at plan | 263,191.24 a year, before burden |
| Depreciation at plan | 293,499.96 a year |
| Practical hours of one position | 80% × 8 hours × the 2026 working days |
| Severance per position | Eight 40-hour weeks of straight-time pay with burden |
| Materiality for the statements | 5% of income before income taxes as recorded |
| Margin floor for pricing | 40% gross margin on time-driven cost, before unused capacity |
| Demand-growth test (optional) | Volume 40% and 50% above 2026 |

: The controller's planning assumptions {#tbl-18-02}


## The Data You Will Use

Much of what you need you have already built. Chapter10.sql and Chapter11.sql measured the plant's hours against standard, and the plan figures in @tbl-18-02 are the plant's plan for 2027, which the Part III case built if you completed it. Chapter 7 taught regression, Goal Seek, Data Tables, and Solver, and Chapter 15 built a disconnected table that switches a measure, which you will use again. Exercise 8.6 tested the price lists, and Chapter 7 asked whether a promotion raised volume.

The case also draws on tables the chapters used little or not at all. Item carries each product's standard cost and its parts: labor, variable and fixed overhead, conversion cost, standard labor hours, and whether it is manufactured or purchased (SupplyMode); material is standard cost less conversion cost. Routing and RoutingOperation give each product's setup hours per work order and run hours per unit at each work center, and WorkCenter and WorkCenterCalendar give the hours each work center had available. ProductionCompletionLine carries the standard cost released by each completion, part by part. PayrollRegisterLine tells regular, overtime, and salary earnings apart, and Employee.PayClass tells hourly from salaried staff. PriceList and PriceListLine hold the price lists, and PurchaseOrderLine what Charles River pays for the products it buys.

You will keep three files, listed in @tbl-18-03.

| Tool | File | Holds | Hand-off |
|--------|------------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| SQL | MakeBuy.sql, run on CharlesRiver_Capstone.sqlite | Family results, the inputs to 1090, activities, capacity | Copy with Headers or Export to CSV |
| Excel | Make Buy Reprice.xlsx | Assumptions, cost behavior, costs, make or buy, capacity, prices, standards, documentation | A Table of item costs |
| Power BI | Product Costs.pbix | The explorer for the meeting, with a Validation page and a Tests tab | Reads the workbook and CharlesRiver.xlsx |

: Tools and files {#tbl-18-03}

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Units and populations need care in this case. Group products into families by the first seven characters of the item code: the three-letter product type of Chapter 5 is not enough, because FUR-TBL is a dining table and LGT-TBL is a table lamp. Quantities are fractional, so add them; never count rows as units. The variance closed in 2026 includes work completed in 2025, and some work orders are still open, so state which units you divide by. Design services carry a standard cost of zero, so leave them out. And the finished goods on hand at the opening of the ledger carry no item detail, so stock by item can be rebuilt only from what was made and shipped since then.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Some records cannot carry this analysis. Part III found that direct time recorded by work center moved toward packing and quality assurance and was often recorded after the operation had ended, so use the routings' standard times, not the time recorded, to measure what each family uses. The overhead variance that each work order's close records moves with that work order's actual direct labor cost, so a family's share of it is an allocation, not a measurement of what the family consumed. Payroll posts on its pay dates, so some months carry three payrolls (Chapter 11), and January 2024 was a start-up month that distorts any monthly trend it enters.
:::


## Getting Started

Set up your files before you begin. Make a working copy of the downloaded CharlesRiver.sqlite named CharlesRiver_Capstone.sqlite, and open the copy in DB Browser for SQLite, so that the download is never changed and the CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite of Part III keeps its views. Start MakeBuy.sql with a header comment that states its purpose, the database file, the preparer and the date, and the checks it performs, and write two comment lines above every query: what it tests, and its population and expected result. Create Make Buy Reprice.xlsx with an Assumptions sheet that holds @tbl-18-01 and @tbl-18-02 and a Documentation sheet that states the purpose, the sources, and the date through which the data run, and create Product Costs.pbix. You need DB Browser for SQLite, Excel for Microsoft 365 with the Solver add-in if you take the optional part of Requirement 7, and Power BI Desktop, which runs only on Windows; if you work on a Mac, plan to use a Windows computer for Requirement 5.

Work in four milestones, one for each phase of the requirements. Your instructor may ask you to hand in each milestone and may then release checkpoint values, so that an early error does not carry through the rest of the case.

1. **What the records show** (Requirements 1 to 3): the family results, the inputs to 1090 with their behavior tests, and the capacity table.
2. **What a product costs** (Requirements 4 and 5): the three costs for each family, the unused capacity reconciled to 1090, and the explorer.
3. **Make, buy, or reprice** (Requirements 6 to 8): the decision for each quoted family, the value of freed capacity, and the price increases.
4. **Standards and the memo** (Requirements 9 and 10): the revised standard, its effect on the statements, and the memo.

## Requirements

The requirements fall into four phases: what the records show, what a product costs, whether to make, buy, or reprice, and how the standards should change. Each phase uses what the one before it found.

### Phase 1: What the Records Show

**Requirement 1: Test the CFO's numbers and the premises behind them (Chapters 9 to 11).**

The CFO's comparison joins invoice lines, items, work orders, their closes, and completions, and every one of those joins can fan out. It is a query, written once and reconciled to the ledger before anyone reads a margin from it.

- In MakeBuy.sql, for each manufactured family in fiscal 2026, return the units sold, revenue, list value, and standard cost; the variance of the year's closes, by material, labor, and overhead, and as a share of the standard cost completed; and the variance per unit completed.
- Compute three margins for each family: at standard, after the variance per unit completed, and with the year's whole variance charged, as the ledger charges it. Set the purchased products of the same family beside them.
- Test the CFO's second premise: whether list prices and standard costs changed at any time in the three years.
- Reconcile the families' variances to account 5080.

**Requirement 2: Take the overhead apart (Chapters 7, 10, and 11).**

"Overhead at a third of its cost" is a claim about cost behavior, and cost behavior is tested, not assumed. SQL extracts what flowed into account 1090 and what the standards released from it; the regressions belong in the workbook, as in Chapter 7.

- Split the 2026 inputs to 1090 into direct and indirect labor, regular and overtime, salaries, employer taxes and benefits, the Factory Overhead entries, and depreciation, and set them against the standard cost that completions released, by labor and overhead. Express both per standard hour.
- Extract each input by month, January 2024 to December 2026, with the standard hours completed each month, and test which inputs move with output from February 2024 on. Explain what including January 2024, and the months with three pay dates, would do to the test.
- Write a sentence for each input that classifies it as a cost that varies with output, a committed capacity cost, or neither, with the evidence.

**Requirement 3: Measure the activities and the capacity (Chapters 10 and 11).**

What each family uses of the plant comes from the routings, multiplied by what was made; what the plant had comes from its calendar. Both are joins and sums over the year's work orders, which SQL handles directly.

- For each family's 2026 completions, return the work orders, units, average batch size, run hours and setup hours by work center, and material issue lines, and express setup hours and issue lines per thousand units.
- For each work center, return the hours available in 2026, the practical capacity under @tbl-18-02, the routing time used, and its share of each.
- Explain in a sentence why routing time is the right measure of use here, and what it leaves out.

### Phase 2: What a Product Costs

Three costing views answer different questions, as @fig-18-01 shows. Standard costing charges each product a rate per standard hour and sends everything else to the variance account. Actual absorption spreads the year's whole cost over the units made, so a product's cost rises whenever the plant runs below capacity. Time-driven costing charges each product for the capacity it uses at the cost of practical capacity, and reports the capacity left unused as a cost of the plant. If supplying an hour of practical capacity costs 40 and a product's routing takes 1.5 hours a unit, setup included, the product carries 60 of conversion cost, however much of its capacity the plant uses that year.

![Three ways to cost the plant's time.](/visuals/svg/fig-18-01-costing-views.svg){#fig-18-01 fig-alt="A diagram of three costing views fed by what the plant paid for in a year: crew, supervision, equipment, and factory overhead. Standard costing charges products the standard rate times standard hours and leaves a variance, charged to cost of goods sold. Actual absorption charges products all of the year's cost divided by the units made and leaves nothing out, so idle time is spread into every unit. Time-driven costing charges products a capacity cost rate times the routing time used, plus factory overhead, and reports unused capacity as a cost of the plant."}

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Time-driven activity-based costing asks two questions: what each unit of capacity costs, and how much capacity each product or customer uses. Kaplan and Anderson (2004) suggest, as a rule of thumb, that practical capacity is 80% to 85% of theoretical capacity. Cooper and Kaplan (1992) had argued that activity-based systems measure the cost of the resources used, so that the difference between the resources a company supplies and those it uses appears as the cost of unused capacity. Measuring cost on practical capacity, rather than on the volume actually produced, keeps that cost out of the products and makes it visible to the managers who can act on it.
:::

**Requirement 4: Compute three costs for each family (Chapter 7).**

Each cost is a formula over a handful of inputs that the decision makers will want to change, which makes this workbook work: one Assumptions sheet, every cost a formula, and every assumption a cell.

- Compute each manufactured item's cost under the three views. Standard is the item's standard cost. Actual absorption adds its family's variance per unit completed. Time-driven costs material, with the 2026 material variance as a rate; the Factory Overhead entries per standard hour; and the committed costs of the crew (every hourly manufacturing employee), supervision, and equipment per hour of practical capacity, times the item's routing time per unit, with setup spread over the family's average batch.
- Show the unused capacity as its own line, and reconcile the products' costs plus the unused capacity to the inputs to 1090.
- Summarize by family at the 2026 mix of items sold, with the margin under each view, and find the share of margin the top fifth of items earns under each.
- Add a Data Table of practical capacity from 75% to 90% of available hours, and explain what moves and what barely moves. Excel takes a data table's input cell only from the table's own worksheet, so keep the practical share that the cost formulas use in a cell on that sheet.
- Keep the item costs as an Excel Table, so that Power BI can load them.

### Phase 3: Make, Buy, or Reprice

The test for one family is in @fig-18-02. What matters is which costs stop if Charles River stops making the family. Materials and the overhead that varies with output stop at once. The crew's time stops costing money only if the crew is reduced; otherwise buying adds the supplier's price to costs the company keeps paying.

![The make-or-buy test for one family.](/visuals/svg/fig-18-02-make-or-buy-test.svg){#fig-18-02 fig-alt="A flowchart for one family. If the delivered quote, price plus inbound freight, is below materials plus factory overhead, buy if the terms, quality, and minimum volume are acceptable. If not, but it is below that cost plus the crew time the family uses, buy only if the crew will be reduced in step with the hours freed, weighing tooling and severance over the quote's two years; if the crew stays, keep making. If the quote is above both, keep making and test the price against the margin floor, repricing if it falls below."}

**Requirement 6: Decide make or buy, family by family (Chapter 7).**

The comparison is a few lines per family, with two assumptions that the decision turns on: the quote and what happens to the crew. A workbook lets the decision makers change both and watch the answer move.

- For each quoted family, compute the relevant cost per unit with the crew kept, which is materials and the overhead that varies, and with the crew reduced in step with the hours freed, which adds the crew's cost of the routing time. Compare each with the delivered quote, and compute the annual effect at the 2026 volume.
- Add the one-time costs for the families you would buy: tooling, and severance for the positions no longer needed under @tbl-18-02. Show the effect over the two years the prices are fixed.
- Use Goal Seek for the quote at which each family breaks even under each crew case, and build a two-way Data Table of the quote, 10% either side, against the share of the freed crew time actually removed, for the families you would buy taken together.
- Set the CFO's absorption view beside your answer, and explain in two sentences why the two disagree.
- List the terms that the numbers leave out.

::: {.callout-warning .watch-out icon=false}
## Watch out
Actual absorption cost is not a relevant cost. It includes supervision, depreciation, and the crew's idle hours, which do not stop when one family is bought. If a family goes and those costs stay, they fall on the families that remain, which then look more expensive and invite the next decision to buy: the spiral that cost systems built on actual volume can set off. Compare the quote with the costs that would stop, and state what has to happen for each of them to stop.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .in-practice icon=false}
## In Practice
Price is the most powerful lever on profit, and often the least managed. In a study of companies with average economics, a 1% improvement in price, with no loss of volume, raised operating profit by 11.1%, three to four times the effect of a 1% gain in volume (Marn & Rosiello, 1992). The authors traced how the price a customer finally pays falls from the list price through discounts to the invoice price, and then through cash discounts, allowances, rebates, and freight to what they called the pocket price. Chapter 15's gross-to-net waterfall did the same for Charles River, from list price to net revenue.
:::

### Phase 4: Standards and the Memo

**Requirement 9: Revise the standards, and measure what they mean for the statements (Chapter 9).**

Standards serve inventory as well as decisions. The inventory standard of U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (Financial Accounting Standards Board Accounting Standards Codification Topic 330) allocates fixed production overhead on the normal capacity of the facilities and charges abnormal costs, such as idle facility expense, to the period. The workbook can rebuild a standard from the plan in @tbl-18-02 and revalue the stock it applies to.

- Propose a standard conversion rate per standard hour on normal capacity, the plan volume of @tbl-18-02 at its hours per standard hour: the labor rate with burden for the direct and the normal indirect hours, the overhead that varies, and the plan's supervision and depreciation spread over the plan volume. Compare it with the current rate, the time-driven rate, and 2026's actual cost, and explain why a standard built on 2026's actual cost would carry idle capacity into inventory.
- Revalue the manufactured finished goods made since the ledger opened and still on hand at the end of fiscal 2024, 2025, and 2026, and measure the effect on retained earnings at the start of fiscal 2025, on 2025 and 2026 income, and on each balance sheet, against the materiality of @tbl-18-02. Show how the answer depends on what you treat as normal capacity.
- The company issued its fiscal 2025 and 2026 statements to its shareholders. Recommend whether the correction belongs in the next statements or calls for revised ones, and what the CFO should tell the shareholders.

## Deliverables and Checklist

Before you submit, check that you have each of these:

1. MakeBuy.sql, with its header complete and two comment lines above every query.
2. Make Buy Reprice.xlsx, with the Assumptions sheet holding the quote and every assumption in @tbl-18-02; sheets for cost behavior, costs, make or buy, capacity, prices, and standards; and the Documentation sheet with the date through which the data run.
3. Product Costs.pbix, with its About and Validation pages and its Tests tab.
4. The memorandum, of no more than two pages, with its decision table and an appendix of exhibits of no more than three pages.


## What a Strong Submission Includes

- Every figure reconciled to account 5080 and to the inputs to 1090, with the populations and units stated.
- Cost behavior tested before any cost is called variable or committed, with the records that cannot carry the test named.
- A different cost for each question: absorption for neither decision, relevant costs for make or buy, time-driven costs for pricing, and standards on normal capacity for inventory (Noreen, 1991; Balakrishnan et al., 2012a).
- The crew assumption made explicit, with the break-even quotes and the one-time costs.
- Price increases set beside the volume they can afford to lose and the evidence on how customers respond.
- Standards proposed on a stated capacity, with their effect on the fiscal 2026 statements measured and reported to the CFO.
- Files that someone else could rerun, and a memo that two people who disagree can act on.

::: {.callout-note .connecting-dots icon=false}
## Connecting the Dots
This case brought back earlier answers. Chapters 10 to 12 found that the plant pays for hours beyond its work; here those hours became the unused capacity that no product should carry. Chapter 7 found that a promotion needed more lift than the orders showed, which is part of the evidence the price increases rest on. And the fiscal 2026 statements come back too, because a cost study can change what the statements should have said.
:::


## Looking Ahead

This case asked what the plant's products cost, and found that the answer depends on the question. Requirements 1 and 3 were descriptive analytics, in the terms of @tbl-01-01: what the families earned and what they used of the plant. Requirements 2 and 4 were diagnostic: why the variance grew and where the cost really sits. Requirements 7 and 8 were predictive, estimating what freed capacity, growth, and higher prices would do. And the recommendations on making, buying, repricing, and the standards were prescriptive, as decisions usually are.

Decisions like these are rarely made once. Quotes expire, crews change, and prices move, so the workbook and the explorer you built are tools for the next round as much as answers to this one. A plant that measures its costs on practical capacity every year sees idle capacity while it is still small, and a company that reviews its standards every year never has to explain three years of stale ones at once.
